claims.sentence: The MHRA has opened a UK-wide consultation on letting schools buy and keep spare adrenaline nasal sprays for emergencies, alongside auto-injectors.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text: UK-wide consultation (MHRA with NI Department of Health) on amending the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 to let schools purchase and hold spare nasal sprays alongside AAIs.

claims.sentence: The MHRA consultation was published on 19 October 2026 and closes on 14 December 2026.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: MHRA published the consultation on 19 October 2026; closes at 11:59pm on 14 December 2026.

claims.sentence: It asks for views on changing the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 so schools can buy and hold spare adrenaline nasal sprays.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: proposed amendments to the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 to allow schools to purchase and hold spare nasal sprays.

claims.sentence: Schools could choose to hold auto-injectors, nasal sprays or both.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: schools could choose AAIs, nasal sprays, or both.

claims.sentence: The existing safeguards would stay in place.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: the existing rules would stay.

claims.sentence: The MHRA has opened a UK-wide consultation on proposals to let schools buy and keep spare adrenaline nasal sprays for the emergency treatment of anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction.
claims.evidence: Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis supported. Retrieved MHRA July 2025 approval page glosses anaphylaxis as 'serious allergic reactions'; 'severe' is a near-synonym, aligned to source wording.
claims.newSentence: The MHRA has opened a UK-wide consultation on proposals to let schools buy and keep spare adrenaline nasal sprays for the emergency treatment of anaphylaxis, a serious allergic reaction.

claims.sentence: Schools can already hold spare adrenaline auto-injectors, and the consultation asks for views on extending the existing legal exemptions to nasal sprays.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text says schools IN ENGLAND are currently permitted to hold spare AAIs; the UK-wide scope of the existing exemption is not stated. 'Extending the existing legal exemptions' wording not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Schools in England can already hold spare adrenaline auto-injectors, and the consultation asks for views on allowing them to hold nasal sprays too.

claims.sentence: Under the proposals, schools could choose to hold auto-injectors, nasal sprays or both, and either product could be used whichever device a pupil was prescribed.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: either device could be used in an emergency whatever device the pupil was prescribed.

claims.sentence: The consultation was published on 19 October 2026 and closes on 14 December 2026.
The MHRA says the existing safeguards would remain: emergency adrenaline could only be given to children known to be at risk of anaphylaxis, and by appropriately trained staff.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: spare devices limited to pupils known to be at risk of anaphylaxis and given by trained school staff. (Minor: 'appropriately' trained not verbatim.)

claims.sentence: School supplies would act as a backup and would not replace the expectation that children carry their own prescribed adrenaline medicine.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: spares are a backup, not a replacement for a pupil's own device.

claims.sentence: The MHRA notes that adrenaline nasal spray was authorised in July 2025, which prompted the question of whether schools should be able to hold it.
claims.evidence: MHRA approval of adrenaline nasal spray (EURneffy) on 18 July 2025 is confirmed. That the consultation notes this, or that the approval 'prompted' the question, is not stated in any retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: The MHRA approved an adrenaline nasal spray in July 2025, the first needle-free emergency treatment for anaphylaxis in the UK.

claims.sentence: The government says it will decide whether and how to proceed after weighing the feedback.
claims.evidence: Nothing in the retrieved text states this.
